This is useful when only a specific field needs literal precision, like an action type in a reducer. It avoids freezing the entire object while still giving the compiler the exact literal it needs.

question: How do optional chaining and nullish coalescing work in typed TypeScript code?
directAnswer: Optional chaining "?." lets you access a property or call a method only if the value before it isn't null or undefined, short-circuiting to undefined otherwise. Nullish coalescing "??" provides a fallback value, but only when the left side is specifically null or undefined, not other falsy values like 0 or empty string. They pair naturally: "user?.name ?? 'Anonymous'" safely reads name and supplies a default. In typed code, the compiler reflects this by narrowing the result type and including undefined where chaining can short-circuit.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Optional chaining is the "?." operator that safely accesses nested members. Nullish coalescing is the "??" operator that returns its right-hand value only when the left is null or undefined.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: They exist to replace verbose and error-prone manual null checks and to fix the bug-prone use of "||" for defaults, which incorrectly treats 0, '', and false as missing.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: "a?.b" evaluates to undefined if a is null or undefined, otherwise to a.b, and it short-circuits the rest of the chain. "x ?? y" returns x unless x is null or undefined, in which case it returns y. TypeScript types the chained expression to include undefined and narrows the coalesced result to exclude null and undefined on the left.

whyImportant: These operators are essential for working safely with optional and nullable data under strict null checks, and the distinction between ?? and || prevents a common class of bugs with falsy-but-valid values.
realWorldExample: Reading a nested config with a sensible default: "const timeout = config?.server?.timeout ?? 5000;" safely traverses possibly-missing objects and uses 5000 only when the value is truly absent, so an explicit timeout of 0 would be respected rather than overridden.

nestedTopics.title: ?? vs ||
nestedTopics.explanation: Logical OR treats all falsy values as missing, so "count || 10" wrongly replaces a valid 0 with 10. Nullish coalescing only falls back on null or undefined, so "count ?? 10" preserves 0. Use ?? for defaults on nullable values.

nestedTopics.title: Optional call and index chaining
nestedTopics.explanation: Optional chaining works for calls "fn?.()" and index access "arr?.[0]", not just property access. This lets you safely invoke possibly-undefined callbacks or index possibly-null collections.

nestedTopics.title: Resulting types include undefined
nestedTopics.explanation: Because a chain can short-circuit, the expression's type gains undefined. So "user?.name" is "string | undefined" even if name is always a string, which the compiler tracks and you often resolve with ??.

followUps.question: Why prefer ?? over || for default values?
followUps.answer: Logical OR falls back whenever the left side is any falsy value, including 0, the empty string, NaN, and false, which are often legitimate values you want to keep. Nullish coalescing only falls back on null or undefined, so it preserves those valid falsy values. Using ?? for defaults avoids subtle bugs like a configured value of 0 being silently replaced by a fallback.

followUps.question: How does optional chaining affect the inferred type of an expression?
followUps.answer: Because the chain returns undefined when it short-circuits, TypeScript adds undefined to the result type. So even if a property is non-optional, accessing it through an optional link makes the whole expression "T | undefined". You typically resolve this by coalescing with ?? or by narrowing with a guard before using the value.

followUps.question: Can you combine optional chaining with the non-null assertion?
followUps.answer: You can, as in "a?.b!", but it's usually contradictory and a code smell: the "?." says the value might be missing while the "!" asserts it isn't. If you genuinely know the value is present you should use a guard or restructure the access; mixing them often signals that the types don't match your runtime assumptions and can hide real null bugs.

question: What are generic default type parameters?
directAnswer: Generic default type parameters let you specify a fallback type for a type parameter when the caller doesn't provide one and it can't be inferred. You write it like "<T = string>", so if no argument is supplied, T becomes string. This makes generic types and functions more convenient to use because common cases don't require explicit type arguments. They work a lot like default function parameters, but at the type level, and they pair well with constraints.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A default type parameter is a type assigned to a generic parameter that the compiler uses when no explicit argument is given and inference doesn't determine one, written as "<T = DefaultType>".
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It exists to reduce boilerplate for the most common usage of a generic, letting consumers omit type arguments while still allowing them to override the default when needed.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When a generic is used without an explicit type argument, the compiler first tries inference; if that yields nothing, it falls back to the declared default. Defaults must come after non-default parameters and can reference earlier parameters or satisfy a constraint, for example "<T extends object = {}>".

whyImportant: Defaults improve API ergonomics, which is why they appear in React's typings (like component props) and many libraries. Understanding them clarifies how generic types behave when arguments are omitted.
realWorldExample: A typed event emitter "class Emitter<Events = Record<string, unknown>>" lets simple consumers write "new Emitter()" and get a sensible default event map, while advanced users supply "new Emitter<MyEvents>()" for precise typing.

nestedTopics.title: Defaults vs constraints
nestedTopics.explanation: A constraint ("extends") limits what types are allowed, while a default ("=") supplies a value when none is given. They can be combined, as in "<T extends string = 'a'>", where the default must itself satisfy the constraint.

nestedTopics.title: Ordering rules
nestedTopics.explanation: Type parameters with defaults must follow those without, mirroring default function parameters. A default can reference parameters declared before it, enabling dependent defaults.

nestedTopics.title: Interaction with inference
nestedTopics.explanation: Inference takes priority over the default. The default only applies when the compiler can't infer the parameter from usage and the caller didn't specify it explicitly.

followUps.question: How do defaults differ from constraints?
followUps.answer: A constraint written with "extends" restricts which types are permissible for the parameter and is enforced for every usage, while a default written with "=" simply provides a fallback type when none is inferred or supplied. You can use both together, in which case the default must satisfy the constraint. In short, constraints say what is allowed and defaults say what to use when nothing is given.

followUps.question: When does the default actually get applied?
followUps.answer: The default is used only when the caller doesn't pass an explicit type argument and the compiler can't infer the parameter from the arguments or context. Inference always takes precedence, so if usage determines the type, the default is ignored. This means defaults mainly matter for generic types used without inference, like "Container<>" style usage, or generic functions called with no inferable argument for that parameter.

followUps.question: Can a default type parameter reference another type parameter?
followUps.answer: Yes, a default can reference type parameters declared earlier in the same list, enabling dependent defaults like "<T, U = T[]>" where U defaults to an array of T. The referenced parameter must appear before the one with the default, following the same left-to-right ordering rule. This is useful for relating parameters so callers only need to specify the primary one.
